title: Cities that refused to end
dek: Some urban lives are measured in centuries of repair. Continuity is a civic technology, not a mood.
speakingPrompts: Pick a city older than the country you live in and explain how it survived a disaster that should have ended it.
Is a rebuilt city the same city? Borrow the Ship of Theseus without naming it until the last sentence.
What should a town refuse to demolish if it wants to remain itself?

blocks.text: A city is a habit of people staying. Stones help, rivers help, but the stubborn fact is institutional: markets reopen, names persist, someone still knows where the well was. Damascus, Athens, Varanasi, Luoyang — lists of “oldest cities” quarrel because archaeology, continuous habitation, and political identity do not share a single clock. The quarrel is useful. It shows that “still here” can mean different kinds of survival.

After earthquake, fire, or conquest, a city may keep its street grain even when façades are new. It may keep a pilgrimage even when the skyline changes. It may keep a legal status, a harbour, a shrine. Geographers talk about path dependence: early choices — a ford, a temple, a rail gauge — constrain later ones. That is why old cities feel layered rather than sequential. You walk through decisions that outlived their makers.

There is nothing automatically virtuous about age. Some longevity is the longevity of extractive ports or contested capitals. The intellectual interest is the mechanism: how a place metabolises shock. Water systems, grain storage, religious calendars, and diasporas that send money home are as much infrastructure as bridges. A city that “refused to end” usually had more than nostalgia. It had a reason to be rebuilt in the same spot.

If you live in a young suburb, the lesson is not to fake ruins. It is to ask what would still gather people if the mall closed: a school, a creek, a weekly market, a room that is free to enter. Continuity is easier to start than to retrofit. The oldest cities are not merely ancient. They are places that kept offering a next morning.

references.title: Cities and the Wealth of Nations
